name: Yusuf Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens in a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the musicians for a community theatre, play piano, record dance cues and coach three young players. I have a master's degree in music and thirty years of shows behind me; actors look at me when a scene changes pace. I like catching a late turn without anyone in the audience noticing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the theatre work fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner has regular shifts at a clinic and our children are grown. We rent and have three months of expenses saved. I earn about the usual musician pay and there are some theatres nearby, though nobody has offered me another music-director post. I use AI daily for cue-list drafts and rehearsal reminders, then check every cue against the stage manager's signed score.

I'd say **live piano cues** still follow an actor's pause.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed show fee.
The **theatre and pupils** should keep paying in mild AI.
do: Confirm **six paid shows** and three pupils; request written cancellation rate.
Check **AI cue lists** against signed scores and save fifteen percent of an extra cleared fee after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while paid dates and household wages hold.
S0.quote: A piano cue still has to follow a live actor's pause.
fieldNote: His **senior direction** and typical pay come with three months saved and some nearby theatres.
Daily **AI cue lists** are checked against signed stage scores and played aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre faster cue lists are useful if paid rehearsal hours stay written beside each scene. A piano cue still has to follow a live actor's pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved and my partner's steady clinic wage cover a delayed show fee. I expect the booked theatre and pupil work to hold in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm six paid shows and my three pupils, and ask for a written cancellation rate. In the first year of this modest change I'll keep checking daily AI cue lists against the signed stage score and save fifteen percent of an extra cleared festival fee after rent, food and piano repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next season. A late cheque is irritating, but the household can carry one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after the lighting fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre moved a show after a lighting fault. We received the rehearsal pay, then waited for the replacement performance date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a cue list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I play the cue against the marked scene and ask the drummer to check a changed bar. A neat list can still put the piano in the wrong moment.

I'd bring **revision fees** to the musicians union before accepting free work.
think: Cues and plans bring **one-quarter** of my own pay.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot replace a recurring fee cut.
do: Bring **ten cue invoices** and revision hours to the union this month.
Seek **written live-cue minimum** if orders fall; trial new checker only after that loss and paid engineer instruction outside shows.
Use **owned nameless score** with theatre-funded paid-use licence/local storage; play suggestions and stop errors/leaks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic cuts to cue income.
S1.quote: A fast check will not book a show.
fieldNote: His **union request** prices actual revision and live-cue work before accepting lower fees.
The **new AI trial** needs paid instruction, private owned score, commercial permission, storage and manual play-through.

steps.text: Bring ten cue invoices and revision hours to musicians union
Request written paid live-cue/preparation minimum if orders fall
Trial checker after orders fall/paid off-show lesson on owned nameless score with funded paid-use licence/local approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre which paid dance-cue and rehearsal-planning hours its new software may replace. I'd take our fee sheet to the musicians union before accepting free revisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded cues and plans bring about a quarter of my own pay. If orders fall, three months saved gives some time, but I cannot replace a monthly quarter with a cleverer file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll total ten cue invoices and bring paid revision hours to the union. In the first year, if orders fall, I'll ask the theatre for a written minimum live-cue and preparation rate and trial a new AI cue checker, which flags mismatched musical entrances, only after paid engineer instruction outside shows, using my own nameless score under a theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage; I'll play every suggested cue and stop wrong changes or leaked files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of cue income. A fast check will not book a show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test on cast rehearsal audio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a cast rehearsal recording is not my test file. I would need written performer consent and a storage rule before any such upload.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the new checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre must pay the engineer and licence without dropping a paid cue hour. I will go back to the marked paper score if a trial costs my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cast that thinking AGI by 2028 could make dance cues before a robot plays the piano. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want signed live-show calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recorded cue and planning fees to end in 2028, taking a quarter of my pay. Live shows might also fall, but they are still booked today and I will not call that second loss certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total cue and planning fees, ask for signed paid show dates and request an actual pension estimate before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid theatre music-director role only if my master's and directing experience qualify, actual live human rehearsal direction and cue supervision is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit its hours; I'll keep current shows and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected quarter of my pay disappearing, with three months saved and some nearby employers giving a search window. I'd be alarmed if live shows collapsed as well, but that is a further condition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is another director job open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No theatre has offered me a director vacancy. I would read a current paid posting with its duties and hours before counting another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a pension estimate. A long career cannot tell me what pension payment will reach our account each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre board that five years to AGI by 2031 gives us time to agree on paid live cue supervision. Playing robots follow around 2034, so actors will still need a human musician watching their timing before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may make recorded cues cheaper before 2031. I can use a checker to prepare, but the theatre must pay for the person who hears an actor depart from the plan on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll propose a written two-year contract with paid live cue supervision, preparation time and cancellation fees, using the union's invoice sheet. In the first year after 2031, if recorded cue fees stop, I'll keep signed paid shows and use an AI cue checker only after a paid engineer lesson outside booked shows, under the theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage on my own nameless score, playing every change and stopping errors or leakage; I will ask the union to compare actual paid cue hours with the contract. If live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid music-director role only if my master's and directing experience qualify, actual live human rehearsal direction and cue supervision is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recorded fees fading, though a live role gives me something to negotiate. A screen cannot watch an actor change the length of a silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the board accepted that contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The board has not accepted the contract. I will count only signed paid calls, not a meeting minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep cast rehearsal audio out of the checker without written consent. The score I own is enough, and I can stop the tool when a cue is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read actual pension figures and signed theatre calls. Piano-playing robots follow around 2039, but a birthday does not pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need paid music direction and pupil fees. Three months saved now and an unknown pension do not tell me when I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid-show plan, then save fifteen percent of each extra cleared festival fee after rent, food and piano repairs toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid theatre and pupil work while booked; if live calls fall and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid music-director role only if my master's and directing history qualify, actual live human rehearsal direction and cue supervision is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant pay mix with current calls and three months saved. I'll slow only when a real pension amount and signed fees cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra festival pays, no part of it goes into savings. I won't take food money to make six months appear in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen the pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't seen our pension statements. I'll compare actual monthly figures with rent before giving up a paid show.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue and planning fees could end before another directing post opens. Signed show dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualified director role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is paid to catch a late actor's cue when the guide track is perfect. A clean cue list does not conduct a live scene.

headlineQuote: A clean cue list does not conduct a live scene.
portrait: Yusuf is a **58-year-old theatre music director** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
His **typical pay**, three-month reserve and some local theatres offer time to respond to cue-fee cuts.
He uses **AI daily** for cues and seeks paid supervised trials on owned nameless scores under licence and manual checks.
He bargains for **paid live cue supervision** while checking actual pension figures before reducing work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a quarter of Yusuf's pay from cues and planning.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed shows**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying directing with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
